concept.technique_name: average rate via total distance over total time (Smart Numbers)

examples.problem_statement: A car travels from Town A to Town B at an average speed of 40 miles per hour, and returns along the same route at an average speed of 50 miles per hour. What is the approximate average speed in miles per hour for the entire trip?

solution.result: the quantity to build is total distance divided by total time
solution.description: Set up the average-rate relationship the book uses: on average rate problems you do not average the two speeds, you find the total distance and divide by the total time.
Choose a Smart Number for the one-way distance d. The book picks 200 miles because it is a common multiple of the two rates, 40 and 50, so both leg times come out whole.
Find the time for the outbound leg by dividing the chosen distance by the outbound rate of 40 miles per hour.
Find the time for the return leg by dividing the same distance by the return rate of 50 miles per hour.
Add the two leg times to get the total time for the two trips, exactly as the book totals them.
Add the two equal one-way distances to get the total distance for the two trips, which the book states as 400 miles.

Divide the total distance by the total time to get the average rate for the entire trip. Note it lands below the midpoint 45, because with equal distances the average rate is always weighted toward the slower rate, where more time is spent.

key_reminders: Average rate is total distance divided by total time, never the plain average of the two rates.
When the distance is unknown but the rates are fixed, pick a Smart Number for the distance that is a common multiple of the rates.
With equal distances the average rate is always pulled toward the slower rate, since more time is spent at that rate.
common_mistakes: Averaging 40 and 50 to get 45, which ignores that more time is spent at 40 miles per hour.
Adding the distances but forgetting the trip covers 400 miles, not 200, when dividing by the 9-hour total.

concept.technique_name: standard deviation from squared differences about the mean

examples.problem_statement: Set S = \{-1, 4, 30, -21\}. If the mean = 4, then the standard deviation, rounded to the nearest tenth, is equal to

solution.description: Take the difference between the mean, 4, and the first term, -1, and square it. The book works this one out explicitly as the model for the rest.
Repeat the squared-difference computation for the term 4; the printed solution records this term's contribution as 16.
Take the difference between the mean and the term 30, giving -26, and square it. Squaring removes the sign, so the negative difference contributes a positive amount.
Take the difference between the mean and the term -21, giving 25, and square it. Subtracting a negative widens the gap, which is why this term contributes so heavily.
Add all four squared differences together to get the single total the book carries forward.
Take the square root of that total, using the on-screen calculator as the book directs.
Round the square root to the nearest tenth, because the question asked for that precision.

key_reminders: Work from differences about the mean, and square each difference so signs do not cancel.
Subtracting a negative term from the mean widens the difference: 4 - (-21) = 25, not -17.
Round only at the end, to the precision the question names.
common_mistakes: Mishandling 4 - (-1) and 4 - (-21) as subtraction of positives, losing the two largest contributions.
Rounding \sqrt{1342} to 36.7 or truncating to 36.6 without checking the digit after the tenths place.

concept.technique_name: combinations with the multiplication principle across two independent picks

examples.problem_statement: Lothar has 6 stamps from Utopia and 4 stamps from Cornucopia in his collection. He will give two stamps of each type to his friend Peggy Sue. Quantity A: the number of ways Lothar can give 4 stamps (two of each type) to Peggy Sue. Quantity B: 100. Choose: (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.operation: \text{two successive pick-a-group problems: choose 2 of 6, then 2 of 4}
solution.result: one Utopian selection and one Cornucopian selection
solution.description: Frame the task the way the book does: Lothar picks 2 out of his 6 Utopian stamps, and then separately picks 2 out of his 4 Cornucopian stamps.
Apply the combinations formula to the Utopian stamps to count the groups of size 2 that can be drawn from 6; order within the group does not matter.
Apply the same combinations formula to the Cornucopian stamps to count the groups of size 2 drawn from 4.
Multiply the Utopian result by the Cornucopian result, since each Utopian pair can be paired with any Cornucopian pair, giving Quantity A.
Compare Quantity A, 90, against Quantity B, 100, and select the choice stating that Quantity B is greater.

key_reminders: Use combinations, not permutations: the two stamps handed over form a group, so order does not matter.
Two independent selections combine by multiplying their counts, not adding them.
common_mistakes: Adding 15 + 6 = 21 instead of multiplying, which would flip the comparison the wrong way.
Treating the picks as ordered (6 \times 5 \times 4 \times 3) and getting a count above 100, leading to choice (A).
